title: Load and unload horses for and from transport

lessons.title: Preparing horses for transport
lessons.html:
Why preparation matters

Travel is stressful for horses. They must balance in a moving vehicle, they cannot see where they are going, and they are in a small space. Good preparation keeps the horse safe and calm and reduces injuries and travel sickness.

Check the horse

  • Is the horse fit to travel? Do not load a horse that is lame, sick, or has a high temperature unless the vet says so.
  • Check the identity: the right horse, with its passport or movement documents if needed.
  • Give water before the trip. Follow the trainer's or manager's instructions about feeding.

Travel clothing

ItemProtects
Headcollar (leather or with a breakable part) and lead ropeControl while loading and tying
Travel boots or bandages with paddingLegs from knocks and treading on themselves
Tail bandage or tail guardTail from rubbing on the ramp or back of the box
Poll guard (if used)Top of the head if the horse throws its head up
Light sheet or cooler, depending on weatherKeeps the horse comfortable; avoid overheating

Fit boots so they do not slip. Put travel boots on the horse in the stable, then walk it a few steps so it gets used to them.

Check the vehicle

  1. Is the floor solid and covered with rubber mats or bedding so it is not slippery?
  2. Is the ramp strong and are the springs and hinges working?
  3. Are partitions and breast bars secure?
  4. Is there a string loop on each tie ring?
  5. Is there a full hay net (if allowed) and a water container for the trip?
  6. Are the tow hitch, lights and tyres checked by the driver?

Park the horse box on level ground, with the ramp on firm footing, next to a wall or fence if possible so the horse has fewer ways to step off the side.

People and protective clothing

Handlers wear gloves, boots and preferably a helmet. Never load alone; you need at least one helper. Plan who leads, who closes the partition and who lifts the ramp.

lessons.title: Loading horses safely
lessons.html:
Loading step by step

  1. Open the vehicle and make the inside light and inviting. Open the front ramp or groom's door if there is one, so the horse sees light.
  2. Move the partition across to make more space, if the vehicle allows.
  3. Lead the horse straight towards the centre of the ramp, walking at its shoulder and looking ahead, not at the horse.
  4. Walk up the ramp with confidence. Do not stop and pull.
  5. Once the horse is in, the helper puts up the breech bar or closes the partition behind it. Only then tie the horse up.
  6. Tie to a string loop with a quick-release knot, with the rope long enough for the horse to balance with its head but not so long it can turn or bite its neighbour.
  7. Lift and secure the ramp. Stand to the side of the ramp, never directly behind it or behind the horse.

Important order: breech bar first, then tie up. If you tie first and the horse runs back, it can panic and injure itself.

A horse that will not load

  • Stay calm and patient. Shouting and hitting make it worse.
  • Give the horse time to look and sniff.
  • Load a calm companion horse first.
  • Put feed in a bucket inside.
  • Two helpers can hold a lunge line around the hindquarters (above the hocks) to encourage the horse forward, standing well to the sides.
  • Ask an experienced handler if the horse still refuses.

When loading more than one horse

In a two-horse trailer with one horse, load it on the side that keeps the weight on the crown of the road, as your yard instructs. Load the quietest horse first. Keep horses that do not get on apart.

During the journey

The driver must drive smoothly: brake gently, take corners slowly, and avoid sudden stops. On long trips stop every few hours to check the horses and offer water.

Safety rules

  • Never stand directly behind a horse or a ramp.
  • Never wrap a rope around your hand.
  • Never get into a trailer compartment with a frightened horse without an exit.
  • Never travel horses loose in an open bakkie.

lessons.title: Unloading horses safely
lessons.html:
Unloading step by step

  1. Park on level, firm ground away from traffic, with space in front of the ramp. Check there is nothing sharp or slippery where the horse will step.
  2. Speak to the horses so they know you are there.
  3. Lower the ramp slowly, standing to the side.
  4. Untie the horse first, then open the breech bar or partition. This is the opposite order to loading. A horse that moves back while still tied can panic.
  5. Guide the horse to walk down the ramp straight and slowly. Stay at its shoulder. Do not let it rush or jump off the side.
  6. If it is a front-unload vehicle, lead the horse forward down the front ramp.
  7. Walk the horse a few steps on the ground to let it stretch and settle.

After unloading: check the horse

  • Look for cuts, scrapes and swelling, especially on legs, hips and the head.
  • Check it walks sound.
  • Look at breathing and sweating. Heavy sweating, fast breathing, a cough, nasal discharge or dullness after a long trip may be signs of travel sickness, which can be serious. Report it at once and take the horse's temperature if you are trained.
  • Offer water.
  • Remove boots, bandages and tail guard. Check the skin under them.

At the destination

Put the horse in a clean, safe stable or camp. Check that the water is clean and the fences and doors are safe. New arrivals may need to be kept apart from other horses for a while, as the yard manager decides.

After the trip

  1. Muck out the vehicle. Remove dung and wet bedding.
  2. Wash the floor and check it for damage.
  3. Clean and dry the boots and travel gear and pack them away.
  4. Report any damage to the vehicle or equipment.
  5. Complete any travel records the yard keeps.

Key points

  • Only travel horses that are fit; fit boots, tail guard and headcollar.
  • Check the vehicle floor, ramp, partitions and string loops before loading.
  • Loading: breech bar first, then tie. Unloading: untie first, then open the bar.
  • Never stand directly behind a horse or a ramp.
  • After unloading, check for injuries and signs of travel sickness and clean the vehicle.
